SK2141 The argument replaces what the caller-info attribute would have supplied

An explicit argument is passed to a [CallerMemberName], [CallerLineNumber], [CallerFilePath] or [CallerArgumentExpression] parameter, suppressing the substitution the parameter exists for.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperExplicitCallerInfoArgument (resharper_explicit_caller_info_argument_highlighting)

Why

Caller-info substitution happens only when the argument is omitted. Supply one and the compiler steps back silently: the parameter still has a value, the call still compiles, and the diagnostic the parameter was added to carry is now whatever the caller typed. For [CallerLineNumber] and [CallerFilePath] that is a fabricated source location — a log line, an assertion message or an exception that names a place the code is not — and it is the one class of wrong data that survives review indefinitely, because nobody re-derives a line number by hand. ⚠ This rule and `SK0232` share a span and must not disagree about it. SK0232 excludes caller-info parameters from its redundant-argument scan precisely because passing null to one is the opposite of redundant: omit it and the compiler substitutes a name, so the argument is the only thing keeping the value null. The two are disjoint by construction rather than by filter — SK0232 never looks at a caller-info parameter, and this rule reports only arguments that restate the substitution exactly or fabricate a location, never null.

Example

Instead of:

void Run() {
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value, nameof(value));
    Trace("started", nameof(Run));
}

void Trace(string message, [CallerMemberName] string? member = null) { }

Write:

void Run() {
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);
    Trace("started");
}

void Trace(string message, [CallerMemberName] string? member = null) { }

When it does not fire

⚠ The general shape does not ship and the narrowing is the rule. OnPropertyChanged(nameof(Other)) against an [CallerMemberName] parameter is ordinary, correct, extremely common code — raising a change notification for a property other than the one being set is the whole point of the overload — and a rule that reports every explicit argument to a caller-info parameter reports that. So a [CallerMemberName] or [CallerArgumentExpression] argument is reported only when it restates exactly what the compiler would have substituted: a constant string equal to the enclosing member's name, or equal to the source text of the argument the [CallerArgumentExpression] names. Anything else is a deliberate value and is declined. [CallerLineNumber] and [CallerFilePath] are reported for any constant argument, because there is no equivalent deliberate use — nobody hand-writes a line number they mean. ⚠ Forwarding falls out of that rather than needing a guard: a relay passing its own [CallerMemberName] parameter down passes an identifier, which is not a constant, so it is never a candidate. ⚠ Only a trailing run of arguments is reported, dropped in one edit. A caller-info argument followed by an ordinary one cannot be deleted without moving what follows it, and two adjacent caller-info arguments reported separately would make skala fix loop — the same reasoning SK0232 applies to trailing defaults. Named arguments, ref/out arguments and calls supplying more arguments than the method has parameters are declined outright: for those, "the parameter this argument fills" is not a fact. Every candidate deletion is re-bound speculatively and withdrawn unless the same method comes back.
